subject: chemistry
title: Unit 1 summary and memory tips
summary: A condensed revision sheet for all of Unit 1: atoms and periodic trends, metallic, ionic and covalent bonding, the mole, organic families, polymers and green chemistry, with memory tips.
body:
This revision sheet squeezes the whole of Year 11 Chemistry Unit 1 onto one page you can come back to before every test. It covers atoms and the periodic table, the three main types of bonding, counting particles with the mole, organic compounds and polymers, and green chemistry. Read a section, close the page, then try to say the key facts out loud from memory.

## Atoms, isotopes and the periodic table

- An atom has a tiny nucleus of **protons** (+1) and **neutrons** (0), with **electrons** (−1) around it.
- **Atomic number (Z)** = number of protons. It defines the element and never changes in a chemical reaction.
- **Mass number (A)** = protons + neutrons, so neutrons = A − Z.
- An **ion** forms when an atom loses electrons (a positive **cation**) or gains electrons (a negative **anion**). Only the electron number changes. For example ⁵⁶Fe³⁺ has 26 protons, 30 neutrons and 23 electrons.
- **Isotopes** have the same number of protons but different numbers of neutrons. They have the same chemical properties (same electron arrangement) but different masses.
- **Relative atomic mass (Aᵣ)** is the weighted mean of the relative isotopic masses, compared with ¹²C = 12 exactly:

`Aᵣ = Σ(relative isotopic mass × % abundance) ÷ 100`

- Aᵣ has no units, and it always lies between the lightest and heaviest isotope masses, closer to the most abundant one.
- The periodic table is ordered by atomic number. A **group** (column) shares the same number of valence electrons; a **period** (row) number equals the number of occupied shells.
- The **s, p, d and f blocks** show which type of subshell the highest-energy electron is in.

## Electron configuration and periodic trends

- Shells contain subshells: s holds up to 2 electrons, p up to 6, d up to 10, f up to 14.
- Filling order: 1s 2s 2p 3s 3p **4s 3d** 4p. The 4s fills before 3d, but 4s electrons are lost first when transition metals form ions.
- Exceptions to learn: Cr is 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p⁶ 3d⁵ 4s¹ and Cu is 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p⁶ 3d¹⁰ 4s¹.
- **Core charge** = number of protons − number of inner-shell electrons. It equals the number of valence electrons for main-group elements (Na +1, Cl +7).

| Trend | Across a period (left to right) | Down a group |
|---|---|---|
| Core charge | increases | stays the same |
| Atomic radius | decreases | increases |
| First ionisation energy | increases | decreases |
| Electronegativity | increases | decreases |
| Metallic character | decreases | increases |

- Explaining a trend always needs two things: what happens to **core charge** and what happens to the **number of shells** (distance from the nucleus).
- Metals get more reactive down a group (valence electrons easier to lose). Non-metals get more reactive up a group and across a period (electrons easier to gain).

## Metallic bonding

- **Metallic bonding** is the attraction between a lattice of positive metal ions (cations) and a sea of **delocalised electrons**.
- Delocalised electrons move freely, so metals conduct electricity and heat and are lustrous.
- The bonding is **non-directional**, so layers of cations can slide without the bonding breaking: metals are **malleable** and **ductile**.
- Higher cation charge and smaller cations give stronger metallic bonding and usually higher melting points.
- The **reactivity series** (most to least reactive): K, Na, Ca, Mg, Al, Zn, Fe, Sn, Pb, Cu, Ag, Au. A metal displaces the ions of any metal below it.
- **Alloys** (for example steel) contain atoms of different sizes that make layers harder to slide, so they are harder and stronger. **Heat treatment** (annealing, quenching, tempering) changes crystal size and hardness.
- Limitations of the electron-sea model: it cannot explain magnetism, the colours of metals, or the size-dependent properties of **metallic nanoparticles** (1–100 nm).

## Ionic bonding

- Metals lose electrons and non-metals gain electrons, usually reaching a noble gas configuration.
- **Ionic bonding** is the strong, non-directional electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions arranged in a three-dimensional **lattice**.
- Formulas show the simplest ratio of ions that makes the total charge zero. Brackets go around a polyatomic ion when you need more than one: Al₂(SO₄)₃, Ca₃(PO₄)₂, Mg(OH)₂.
- Names: cation first, then anion (chloride, oxide, sulfate, nitrate). Use Roman numerals for metals with more than one ion: iron(III) oxide is Fe₂O₃.
- Properties: high melting points (strong attractions throughout the lattice); hard but **brittle** (shifting a layer lines up like charges, which repel); conduct electricity only when **molten or dissolved**, because only then are the ions free to move.
- Slow cooling or evaporation gives larger crystals.

## Covalent bonding, shape and intermolecular forces

- A **covalent bond** is a shared pair of electrons between non-metal atoms. Bonds can be single, double or triple.
- **Lewis (electron dot) structures** show bonding pairs and lone pairs.
- **VSEPR theory**: electron pairs around a central atom repel and spread out as far as possible. Name the shape from the atoms only.

| Electron groups | Lone pairs | Shape | Example |
|---|---|---|---|
| 2 | 0 | linear | CO₂ |
| 3 | 0 | trigonal planar | BF₃ |
| 4 | 0 | tetrahedral (109.5°) | CH₄ |
| 4 | 1 | pyramidal (about 107°) | NH₃ |
| 4 | 2 | bent (about 104.5°) | H₂O |

- A bond is **polar** when the two atoms have different **electronegativities**. A molecule is polar only if its bond dipoles do not cancel, which depends on shape (CO₂ is non-polar; H₂O is polar).
- **Covalent network lattices**: diamond (each C bonded to 4 others, very hard, non-conductor), graphite (each C bonded to 3 others in layers, delocalised electrons so it conducts), graphene (a single graphite layer) and silicon dioxide. All have very high melting points because strong covalent bonds must break.
- **Intermolecular forces** act between molecules and are much weaker than covalent bonds. Boiling a molecular substance breaks only these forces.
  - **Dispersion forces**: in all molecules; stronger with more electrons and greater contact area.
  - **Dipole–dipole attractions**: between polar molecules.
  - **Hydrogen bonding**: when H is bonded to F, O or N and is attracted to a lone pair on F, O or N of another molecule. It explains the high boiling points of H₂O, NH₃ and HF.

## The mole, formulas and percentage composition

- One **mole** contains 6.02 × 10²³ particles (the **Avogadro constant**, Nₐ).
- **Molar mass (M)** in g mol⁻¹ equals the relative atomic, molecular or formula mass.

`n = m ÷ M` and `n = N ÷ Nₐ`

- Subscripts give mole ratios inside a formula: 1 mol of H₂SO₄ contains 4 mol of O atoms.
- Percentage composition = (mass of the element in 1 mol ÷ molar mass) × 100.
- **Empirical formula** = simplest whole-number ratio of atoms. **Molecular formula** = actual number of atoms in one molecule, a whole-number multiple of the empirical formula.
- Empirical formula method: masses (assume 100 g if given percentages) → moles → divide by the smallest → whole numbers (multiply by 2, 3 or 4 if you get about .5, .33 or .25).
- Molecular formula = empirical formula × (molar mass ÷ empirical formula mass).

## Organic compounds

- Carbon forms four bonds and can make chains, branches and rings.
- A **homologous series** shares a functional group and a general formula, with each member differing by CH₂.

| Family | Functional group | Ending | Example |
|---|---|---|---|
| alkanes | C–C single bonds only | -ane | propane, C₃H₈ (CₙH₂ₙ₊₂) |
| alkenes | C=C | -ene | but-2-ene, CH₃CH=CHCH₃ (CₙH₂ₙ) |
| alkynes | C≡C | -yne | ethyne, C₂H₂ (CₙH₂ₙ₋₂) |
| haloalkanes | –F, –Cl, –Br, –I | chloro-, bromo- (prefix) | chloromethane, CH₃Cl |
| alcohols | –OH (hydroxyl) | -ol | propan-1-ol, CH₃CH₂CH₂OH |
| carboxylic acids | –COOH (carboxyl) | -oic acid | ethanoic acid, CH₃COOH |
| esters | –COO– | -yl -oate | ethyl ethanoate, CH₃COOCH₂CH₃ |

- Chain prefixes: meth (1), eth (2), prop (3), but (4), pent (5), hex (6), hept (7), oct (8).
- Alkanes are **saturated**; alkenes and alkynes are **unsaturated** and undergo addition reactions.
- Boiling points rise with chain length (more dispersion forces). Alcohols and carboxylic acids boil higher than alkanes of similar size because of hydrogen bonding.
- When naming an ester, the part from the alcohol comes first (ethyl) and the part from the acid comes second (ethanoate).

## Polymers

- **Polymers** are very long chains of repeating units made from small **monomers**.
- **Addition polymerisation**: alkene monomers join as one bond of each C=C opens; no other product forms. Ethene → polyethene; chloroethene → PVC; tetrafluoroethene → PTFE; propene → polypropene.
- To find the monomer, take the two-carbon repeating unit and put a C=C between the two carbons.
- **Condensation polymerisation**: monomers with two functional groups join and release a small molecule such as water (polyesters, nylon).
- **LDPE** is highly branched, so chains cannot pack closely: soft, flexible, lower density. **HDPE** has little branching, chains pack closely and dispersion forces are stronger: stiffer and stronger.
- **Thermoplastics** have no cross-links and soften on heating, so they can be remelted and recycled. **Thermosets** have covalent **cross-links** and do not soften; they char when heated strongly.
- Most plastics come from fossil fuels. **Bioplastics** come from renewable feedstocks but are not automatically biodegradable. Recycling can be mechanical (remelting) or chemical (back to monomers).

## Green chemistry and the research investigation

- **Green chemistry** designs products and processes that reduce or remove hazardous substances, preventing problems at the design stage.
- The 12 principles: prevention; atom economy; less hazardous syntheses; safer chemicals; safer solvents and auxiliaries; energy efficiency; renewable feedstocks; reduce derivatives; catalysis; design for degradation; real-time analysis; inherently safer chemistry.
- A **linear economy** is take → make → use → dispose. A **circular economy** keeps materials in use through reuse, repair and recycling.

`Atom economy (%) = (molar mass of desired product ÷ molar mass of all reactants) × 100`

- Use the coefficients from the balanced equation. Addition reactions have 100% atom economy. Atom economy is not the same as percentage yield.
- Research investigation: narrow a topic to a focused question, judge sources (the CRAAP test: currency, relevance, authority, accuracy, purpose), watch for bias and greenwashing, reference every source, and finish with an evidence-based conclusion and its limitations.

## Tips to remember

- **Same P, different N**: isotopes have the same Protons but different Neutrons. "Iso" means "same", as in same place on the periodic table.
- **Neutrons = big number − small number** (A − Z). The charge on an ion only ever changes the electron count.
- **4s is first in, first out**: it fills before 3d, but it is the first to lose electrons when a transition metal forms an ion. **Chromium and copper cheat**: they take an electron from 4s to get a half-full (3d⁵) or full (3d¹⁰) d subshell.
- **Across = tighter grip, down = more shells**: going across a period, core charge rises and the same number of shells is pulled in tighter, so atoms shrink and hold electrons harder. Going down, extra shells push valence electrons further out, so they are easier to remove.
- **Bonding in three pictures**: metals = "marbles in glue" (cations in a sea of electrons that flows when layers slide); ionic = "a checkerboard of + and −" (shift one row and like charges line up, so it shatters); covalent molecules = "strong pairs, weak friendships" (strong bonds inside molecules, weak forces between them).
- **Conductivity check**: ask "Is anything charged free to move?" Electrons in metals and graphite, yes; ions in molten or dissolved ionic compounds, yes; ions in solid salt or molecules in sugar, no.
- **H-FON**: hydrogen bonding needs H bonded to F, O or N. If you cannot find H–F, H–O or H–N in the molecule, there is no hydrogen bonding.
- **Polar molecule test (a made-up memory trick: "polar bonds plus lopsided shape")**: both are needed. CO₂ has polar bonds but is symmetrical, so it is non-polar.
- **The mole triangle**: write m on top and n × M underneath. Cover the one you want: n = m ÷ M, m = n × M, M = m ÷ n.
- **Empirical formula rhyme (a made-up memory trick)**: "Percent to mass, mass to mole, divide by small, multiply till whole."
- **Monkeys Eat Peeled Bananas** for meth, eth, prop, but (1 to 4 carbons). After that the prefixes match shapes you know: pent (pentagon, 5), hex (hexagon, 6), hept (7), oct (octopus, 8).
- **Esters are named "alcohol first, acid last"**, like a surname at the end: ethyl ethanoate is made from ethanol and ethanoic acid.
- **HDPE = Hardly branched, Dense, Packed** (a made-up memory trick). LDPE = lots of branches, like a messy pile of twigs that cannot pack.
- **ThermoPLASTIC is like chocolate, thermoSET is like a cake**: chocolate melts and can be reshaped; once a cake is baked (cross-linked), heating it again only burns it.
- **Atom economy = "what you want ÷ everything you put in"**. If an equation has only one product, the atom economy is 100%.
- **If you remember one thing**: structure explains properties. For every property question, name the particles, the bonding or forces between them, and link that to the property.

## Summary

- Atoms are defined by their protons; isotopes differ in neutrons, and Aᵣ is a weighted mean of isotope masses.
- Electron configurations and core charge explain periodic trends in radius, ionisation energy, electronegativity and reactivity.
- Metallic, ionic and covalent bonding each explain a set of properties such as conductivity, malleability, brittleness and melting point.
- VSEPR predicts molecular shape; shape and electronegativity decide polarity, and intermolecular forces control boiling points.
- The mole links mass, particles and formulas: n = m ÷ M and n = N ÷ Nₐ, used for percentage composition and empirical formulas.
- Organic families, addition polymers and green chemistry principles (including atom economy) connect chemistry to a more sustainable future.

questions.prompt: How many protons, neutrons and electrons are in one ³⁷Cl⁻ ion?
questions.explanation: Chlorine has Z = 17, so 17 protons. Neutrons = 37 − 17 = 20. The 1− charge means one extra electron, so 18 electrons. Option A is tempting but gives the electron count of a neutral atom, ignoring the negative charge.

questions.prompt: Gallium has two isotopes: ⁶⁹Ga (relative isotopic mass 68.93, abundance 60.1%) and ⁷¹Ga (relative isotopic mass 70.92, abundance 39.9%). What is the relative atomic mass of gallium?
questions.explanation: Aᵣ = (68.93 × 60.1 + 70.92 × 39.9) ÷ 100 = (4142.69 + 2829.71) ÷ 100 = 6972.40 ÷ 100 = 69.72. Option B (69.93) is the simple average of the two masses, which ignores the different abundances. The answer must be closer to 68.93 because ⁶⁹Ga is more abundant.

questions.prompt: Which is the correct electron configuration of a Fe²⁺ ion (Fe has Z = 26)?
questions.explanation: Fe is 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p⁶ 3d⁶ 4s². When it forms Fe²⁺, the two 4s electrons are lost first, leaving 3d⁶. Option A is tempting because 3d fills after 4s, but the 4s electrons are removed first, not the 3d. Option C is the neutral atom.

questions.prompt: Which statement best explains why the atomic radius decreases from sodium to chlorine across period 3?

options.A: The number of occupied shells decreases across the period.
options.B: Core charge increases while the number of occupied shells stays the same, so valence electrons are pulled closer.
options.C: More electrons are added, and electrons repel each other less as their number increases.
options.D: The number of neutrons increases, which pulls electrons closer to the nucleus.

questions.explanation: Across a period electrons are added to the same (third) shell while core charge rises from +1 to +7, so the valence electrons are attracted more strongly and the atom shrinks. Option A is wrong because all period 3 elements have three occupied shells. Neutrons have no charge, so D is wrong.

questions.prompt: Which property of copper is best explained by the non-directional nature of metallic bonding?

options.C: It can be drawn into wires.
options.D: It reacts with silver nitrate solution.

questions.explanation: Ductility (being drawn into wire) is explained by layers of cations sliding past each other while the sea of delocalised electrons keeps attracting them in every direction, so the bonding is not broken. Option A is tempting, but conductivity is explained by the mobility of delocalised electrons, not by the bonding being non-directional.

questions.prompt: What is the formula of aluminium sulfate?
questions.explanation: Al³⁺ and SO₄²⁻ combine in the ratio 2 : 3 so the charges cancel (2 × +3 = +6 and 3 × −2 = −6). Brackets keep the sulfate ion together: Al₂(SO₄)₃. Option B swaps the numbers, giving a charge of +9 − 4 = +5, which is not neutral.

questions.prompt: Solid sodium chloride does not conduct electricity, but molten sodium chloride does. Why?

options.A: In the molten state the ions are free to move and carry charge.
options.B: Melting breaks covalent bonds and releases free electrons.
options.C: Molten sodium chloride contains delocalised electrons like a metal.
options.D: In the solid the ions have no charge.

questions.explanation: In the solid lattice the ions are fixed in place. When molten, the ions can move, so they carry charge. Option C is the common mix-up with metals: ionic compounds conduct by moving ions, not electrons. NaCl has ionic, not covalent, bonding, so B is wrong.

questions.prompt: What are the shape and polarity of the ammonia molecule, NH₃?
questions.explanation: N has three bonding pairs and one lone pair (four electron groups). The atoms form a pyramid, and because the N–H bonds are polar and the shape is not symmetrical, the dipoles do not cancel, so NH₃ is polar. Option C is tempting because the electron pairs are arranged tetrahedrally, but the shape is named from the atoms only.

questions.prompt: Which of these substances has hydrogen bonding between its molecules?
questions.explanation: Methanol has an H atom bonded directly to O (the –OH group), so hydrogen bonds form between molecules. CH₃F is the tempting answer because it contains both H and F, but the H atoms are bonded to C, not to F, so there is no hydrogen bonding. HCl has dipole–dipole attractions only.

questions.prompt: A compound contains 0.600 g of carbon and 0.200 g of hydrogen. What is its empirical formula?
questions.explanation: n(C) = 0.600 ÷ 12.0 = 0.0500 mol; n(H) = 0.200 ÷ 1.0 = 0.200 mol. Dividing by the smallest gives C : H = 1 : 4, so CH₄. Option C comes from using the mass ratio (0.600 : 0.200 = 3 : 1) instead of the mole ratio.

questions.prompt: What is the name of the compound CH₃CH₂CH₂COOH?
questions.explanation: The chain has four carbons, including the carbon of the –COOH group, so the stem is but-, and the carboxylic acid ending is -oic acid: butanoic acid. Option A is tempting if you forget to count the carbon in the –COOH group.

questions.prompt: Which change would most improve the atom economy of a process?

options.A: Adding a catalyst so the reaction goes faster
options.B: Switching to a reaction in which all the reactant atoms end up in the desired product
options.C: Increasing the percentage yield by reducing losses during filtering
options.D: Running the reaction at a higher temperature

questions.explanation: Atom economy depends only on the balanced equation: the mass of the desired product compared with the mass of all reactants. Only changing the reaction itself changes it, and a reaction with one product has 100% atom economy. Option C is tempting but improves percentage yield, which is a different measure.
